name: Check If Pangram
title: CHECK IF THE SENTENCE IS PANGRAM
statement:
CHECK IF THE SENTENCE IS PANGRAM
Pattern: Set membership

A pangram contains every letter of the English alphabet at least once.
Given a string containing only lowercase English letters, return True
if it is a pangram, otherwise False. Letter order does not matter.

Examples:
    is_pangram("thequickbrownfoxjumpsoverthelazydog") -> True
    is_pangram("leetcode") -> False

Contract: input contains only a-z; repeated letters are allowed.
As a local extension, an empty string returns False. Return a bool.
Uppercase letters, accents, spaces, and punctuation are out of scope.

Think about: how many distinct letters does a complete alphabet have?

Source: https://leetcode.com/problems/check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram/

name: Contains Duplicate
title: CONTAINS DUPLICATE
statement:
CONTAINS DUPLICATE
Pattern: HashSet

Given a list of integers, return True if any value appears at least
twice, and False if every element is distinct.

Examples:
    contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1]) -> True
    contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 4]) -> False

Think about: as you walk through the list, how do you remember which
values you have already seen? What lets you check "have I seen this?"
in one step?
Contract:
Input: a list of integers; it may be empty. Return a bool.

name: Is Subsequence
title: IS SUBSEQUENCE
statement:
IS SUBSEQUENCE
Pattern: Two Pointers

Given two strings `s` and `t`, return True if `s` is a subsequence of
`t`. A subsequence keeps the characters in order but may skip some.
You do NOT rearrange characters.

Examples:
    is_subsequence("abc", "ahbgdc") -> True
    is_subsequence("axc", "ahbgdc") -> False

Think about: walk through `t` with one pointer. Keep a second pointer
on `s`. Every time the current character of `t` matches the character
`s` is waiting for, advance the `s` pointer. Did `s` reach the end?
Contract:
Comparison is case-sensitive; both strings may be empty. Return a bool.

name: Length Of Last Word
title: LENGTH OF LAST WORD
statement:
LENGTH OF LAST WORD
Pattern: String manipulation

Given a string made of words separated by spaces, return the length of
the last word. A word is a maximal substring of non-space characters.
There may be trailing spaces.

Examples:
    length_of_last_word("Hello World")        -> 5
    length_of_last_word("   fly me   to   the moon  ") -> 4
    length_of_last_word("luffy is still joyboy")       -> 6

Think about: trailing spaces can trip you up. How do you isolate the
words and grab the last one? Python string methods can help, but try
to reason about what they do.
Contract:
Input contains only English letters and ordinary spaces, with at least
one word. Empty strings and strings made only of spaces are out of scope.

cases.label: messy spacing
cases.expr: length_of_last_word("   fly me   to   the moon  ")

name: Missing Number
title: MISSING NUMBER
statement:
MISSING NUMBER
Pattern: Math (sum formula) or Set

Given a list containing n distinct numbers taken from the range
0, 1, 2, ..., n (so exactly one number in that range is missing),
return the missing number.

Examples:
    missing_number([3, 0, 1])       -> 2
    missing_number([0, 1])          -> 2
    missing_number([9,6,4,2,3,5,7,0,1]) -> 8

Think about: the numbers 0..n have a known total (n * (n + 1) // 2).
If you compare that to the actual sum of the list, what does the
difference tell you? A Set-based approach also works.
Contract:
The empty list is allowed: n = 0 and the missing number is 0.

name: Single Number
title: SINGLE NUMBER
statement:
SINGLE NUMBER
Pattern: HashMap frequency (or XOR trick)

Every element in the list appears exactly twice, except for one element
that appears only once. Find and return that single element.

Examples:
    single_number([2, 2, 1])       -> 1
    single_number([4, 1, 2, 1, 2]) -> 4

Think about: one simple approach counts how many times each value
appears. A slicker approach uses the XOR property: a ^ a = 0 and
a ^ 0 = a. Try the counting version first, then see if you can do it
without extra memory.
Contract:
The list is non-empty and contains integers (including negatives and zero).
Inputs that break the stated frequency rule are out of scope.

name: Valid Anagram
title: VALID ANAGRAM
statement:
VALID ANAGRAM
Pattern: HashMap (character frequency)

Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters
with the same counts, just in a different order.

Write a function that returns True if `t` is an anagram of `s`,
otherwise False.

Examples:
    is_anagram("anagram", "nagaram") -> True
    is_anagram("rat", "car")         -> False

Think about: how do you compare the contents of two strings while
ignoring the order? What data structure counts things for you?
Contract:
Comparison is case-sensitive and every character counts, including spaces.
Empty strings are allowed. Return a bool.

name: Duplicate Encoder
title: DUPLICATE ENCODER
statement:
DUPLICATE ENCODER
Pattern: HashMap frequency

Convert a string into a new string where each character is replaced by
"(" if it appears only once in the original string, or ")" if it
appears more than once. The check is case-insensitive and spaces count
as characters too.

Examples:
    duplicate_encode("din")    -> "((("
    duplicate_encode("recede") -> "()()()"
    duplicate_encode("Success") -> ")())())"
    duplicate_encode("(( @")    -> "))(("

Think about: you need to know each character's total count BEFORE you
start building the answer. So make one pass to count, then a second
pass to build the output.
Contract:
Input is an ASCII string and may be empty. Return a string.

name: Largest Four
title: LARGEST FOUR
statement:
LARGEST FOUR
Pattern: Sorting / select largest elements

Return the sum of the four largest integers in a list. If there are
fewer than four elements, sum all of them. Repeated values count as
separate elements. Negative values count too; do not discard them.

Examples:
    largest_four([4, 5, -2, 3, 1, 2, 6, 6]) -> 21
    largest_four([1, 2, 3]) -> 6
    largest_four([-5, -2, -3, -4, -1]) -> -10

Contract: input is a list of integers. As a local extension, [] returns 0.
Return an integer. Modifying the input is allowed but not required.

Think about: after sorting, which four positions do you need?
Bonus: keep only the four largest values while scanning once.

Source: recueil_questions.md, Coderbyte Largest Four.

name: Max Sum Distinct Subarray K
title: MAXIMUM SUM OF DISTINCT SUBARRAYS WITH LENGTH K
statement:
MAXIMUM SUM OF DISTINCT SUBARRAYS WITH LENGTH K
Pattern: Sliding Window + frequency map

Given a list of integers and an integer k, look at every contiguous
window of exactly k elements. A window is "valid" only if all k
elements are distinct. Return the largest sum among all valid windows.
If no window of length k has all distinct elements, return 0.

Examples:
    max_distinct_sum([1, 5, 4, 2, 9, 9, 9], 3) -> 15
        windows of size 3: [1,5,4]=10, [5,4,2]=11, [4,2,9]=15,
        [2,9,9] invalid, [9,9,9] invalid -> best valid = 15
    max_distinct_sum([4, 4, 4], 3) -> 0

Think about: slide a window of fixed size k across the list. Keep a
running sum and a frequency map of what is inside the window. When the
window holds k distinct values, it is a candidate. Add the entering
element, remove the leaving one, each step.
Contract:
Input values are positive integers and 1 <= k <= len(nums).
Empty lists and invalid window sizes are out of scope. Aim for O(n) time.

name: Number Stream
title: NUMBER STREAM
statement:
NUMBER STREAM
Pattern: Linear scan / consecutive run length

Given a non-empty string containing only digits from 2 to 9, return the
string "true" if some digit d repeats consecutively at least d times.
Otherwise return the string "false". Count consecutive occurrences,
not the total number of occurrences scattered through the string.

Examples:
    number_stream("6539923335") -> "true"  (three consecutive 3s)
    number_stream("232323")     -> "false"
    number_stream("2222")       -> "true"  (at least two 2s)

Contract: return lowercase strings, as in Coderbyte, not Python booleans.
Digits 0 and 1 and empty strings are outside the input domain.

Think about: remember the previous digit and the current run length.
When the digit changes, the new run starts at one, not zero.

Source: recueil_questions.md, Coderbyte Number Stream.

name: Product Of Array Except Self
title: PRODUCT OF ARRAY EXCEPT SELF
statement:
PRODUCT OF ARRAY EXCEPT SELF
Pattern: Arrays (prefix / suffix products)

Given a list of integers, return a new list where each position holds
the product of every other element (everything except the element at
that position). Do it WITHOUT using division.

Examples:
    product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])  -> [24, 12, 8, 6]
    product_except_self([-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]) -> [0, 0, 9, 0, 0]

Walkthrough of the first example:
    index 0 -> 2*3*4 = 24
    index 1 -> 1*3*4 = 12
    index 2 -> 1*2*4 = 8
    index 3 -> 1*2*3 = 6

Think about: for each index, the answer is (product of everything to
the LEFT) times (product of everything to the RIGHT). Compute the left
products in one pass, the right products in another, and multiply.
Contract:
The input contains at least two integers; negatives and zeros are allowed.
Return a list of integers. Required time: O(n), without division.
Bonus: O(1) extra space, excluding the returned list.

name: Search Insert Position
title: SEARCH INSERT POSITION
statement:
SEARCH INSERT POSITION
Pattern: Binary Search

Given a sorted list of distinct integers and a target value, return the
index of the target if it is found. If not, return the index where it
would be inserted to keep the list sorted.

Examples:
    search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 5) -> 2
    search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 2) -> 1
    search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 7) -> 4
    search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 0) -> 0

Think about: the list is sorted, so you do not need to scan it all.
Keep a low and a high boundary and halve the search space each step.
Where do low and high end up when the target is not present?
Contract:
The list may be empty (return 0). Required time: O(log n).

name: Sort The Odd
title: SORT THE ODD
statement:
SORT THE ODD
Pattern: Arrays / in-place positions

Given a list of integers, sort ONLY the odd numbers in ascending order
while leaving every even number exactly where it is.

Examples:
    sort_odd([5, 3, 2, 8, 1, 4]) -> [1, 3, 2, 8, 5, 4]
    sort_odd([5, 3, 1, 8, 0])    -> [1, 3, 5, 8, 0]
    sort_odd([2, 4, 6])          -> [2, 4, 6]

Walkthrough of the first example:
    odd positions hold 5, 3, 1 (indices 0, 1, 4)
    sorted odds are 1, 3, 5
    drop them back into the same odd positions -> [1, 3, 2, 8, 5, 4]

Think about: collect the odd values, sort them, then place them back
into the slots that originally held an odd value. The even values
never move.
Contract:
Negative integers, zeros, duplicates, and empty lists are allowed.
Return a list; modifying the input is allowed but not required.

name: String Merge
title: STRING MERGE
statement:
STRING MERGE
Pattern: Strings / parallel traversal

The input contains two equally long, non-empty alphanumeric strings
separated by exactly one "*". Return their characters interleaved,
starting with the first character of the left string. Omit the "*".

Examples:
    string_merge("abc1*kyoo") -> "akbyco1o"
    string_merge("aaa*bbb")   -> "ababab"
    string_merge("A*9")       -> "A9"

Contract: the format and equal lengths are guaranteed. Preserve case.
You do not need to validate malformed input or handle unequal lengths.

Think about: split once, then pair characters at matching indices.

Source: recueil_questions.md, Coderbyte String Merge.

name: Triangle Number Check
title: TRIANGLE NUMBER CHECK
statement:
TRIANGLE NUMBER CHECK
Pattern: Math / integer search

A triangular number counts dots arranged in rows of 1, 2, 3, ... dots.
For example, 6 = 1 + 2 + 3. Return True if the input is a triangular
number, otherwise False. The sequence starts 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ...

Examples:
    is_triangle_number(6) -> True
    is_triangle_number(8) -> False
    is_triangle_number(0) -> True

Contract:
Non-negative integers may be very large. Negative numbers and non-integer
values return False. For this Python version, a float such as 6.0 is
accepted as an integer-valued number; 6.5 is not. Strings, None, and bool
values return False. No implicit conversion from text is allowed.

Think about: the total for m rows is m * (m + 1) // 2. Can you search
for m without constructing every previous triangular number? Use exact
integer arithmetic for large integers; floating-point roots can round.

Source: https://www.codewars.com/kata/557e8a141ca1f4caa70000a6

name: Unique In Order
title: UNIQUE IN ORDER
statement:
UNIQUE IN ORDER
Pattern: Linear scan (compare to previous)

Given a string or a list, return a list of items with consecutive
duplicates removed, keeping the original order. Only repeats that are
ADJACENT are collapsed; the same value appearing again later stays.

Examples:
    unique_in_order("AAAABBBCCDAABBB") -> ['A','B','C','D','A','B']
    unique_in_order("ABBCcAD")         -> ['A','B','C','c','A','D']
    unique_in_order([1, 2, 2, 3, 3])   -> [1, 2, 3]

Think about: this is NOT "remove all duplicates". You only drop an item
when it equals the one immediately before it. So you just need to
remember the previous item as you walk through.
Contract:
Input may be a string, list, or tuple; comparison is case-sensitive.
Empty input returns []. Return a list, even for string input.

name: Valid Palindrome
title: VALID PALINDROME
statement:
VALID PALINDROME
Pattern: Two Pointers

A phrase is a palindrome if, after lowercasing and removing every
character that is not a letter or digit, it reads the same forward and
backward. Return True if the input is a palindrome, otherwise False.

Examples:
    is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") -> True
    is_palindrome("race a car")                     -> False
    is_palindrome(" ")                              -> True

Think about: you could clean the string first, then compare it to its
reverse. The two-pointer version is nicer: one pointer from the left,
one from the right, skip non-alphanumeric characters, compare as you
move inward.
Contract:
Input is ASCII and may be empty. Only a-z, A-Z, and 0-9 are retained.

cases.label: classic palindrome
cases.expr: is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")

name: Valid Parentheses
title: VALID PARENTHESES
statement:
VALID PARENTHESES
Pattern: Stack

Given a string containing only the characters ( ) [ ] { }, return True
if every opening bracket is closed by a matching bracket in the correct
order, otherwise False.

Examples:
    is_valid("()")     -> True
    is_valid("()[]{}") -> True
    is_valid("(]")     -> False
    is_valid("([)]")   -> False
    is_valid("{[]}")   -> True

Think about: a closing bracket must match the MOST RECENT unmatched
opening bracket. "Most recent" is the clue: which data structure gives
you back the last thing you put in?
Contract:
The empty string is valid. Return a bool.

name: Valid Triangle
title: VALID TRIANGLE (three side lengths)
statement:
VALID TRIANGLE (three side lengths)
Pattern: Logic (triangle inequality)

The inputs are integers. Zero and negative lengths are invalid.
Three positive lengths can form a valid triangle if the sum of the two
shorter sides is strictly greater than the longest side. Given exactly
three numbers, return True if they can form a triangle, otherwise False.

Examples:
    is_triangle(3, 4, 5)  -> True
    is_triangle(1, 2, 3)  -> False   (1 + 2 is not > 3)
    is_triangle(7, 2, 2)  -> False

Think about: if you sort the three sides, the rule reduces to one
comparison: shortest + middle > longest. Watch the strict inequality.

title: CHALLENGE 1

CHALLENGE 1

An online shop generates an order ID for every purchase. Because of a

recorded today, determine whether the shop issued any ID more than once.

Return True if at least one ID is repeated, False otherwise.

Examples:
    has_repeat([1001, 1002, 1003, 1001]) -> True
    has_repeat([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])          -> False

Contract:
IDs are integers. An empty list returns False.

name: Challenge 02
title: CHALLENGE 2
statement:
CHALLENGE 2

A moderation system flags two usernames as "suspiciously related" when
one is just a rearrangement of the other's characters (same letters,
same counts, possibly the same order). Given two usernames, return True if one

Comparison is exact (case matters, treat every character literally).

    is_rearrangement("listen", "silent") -> True
    is_rearrangement("admin", "demon")   -> False

name: Challenge 03
title: CHALLENGE 3
statement:
CHALLENGE 3

You are given the price of a product recorded once per day, in order.
You may "buy" on one day and "sell" on a later day. Return the maximum
profit you could have made from a single buy-then-sell. If no profit is
possible, return 0.

You cannot sell before you buy.

Examples:
    best_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]) -> 5    (buy at 1, sell at 6)
    best_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1])    -> 0    (prices only fall)

Contract:
Prices are non-negative integers. Fewer than two days returns 0.

name: Challenge 04
title: CHALLENGE 4
statement:
CHALLENGE 4

A search box has an autocomplete feature. It suggests a full product
name only if the letters the user typed appear inside that name in the
same order (other letters may sit between them, but the order must
hold). Given the typed letters and a product name, return True if the
typed letters appear in order inside the name.

Examples:
    matches("abc", "aXbXXc") -> True
    matches("cab", "aXbXXc") -> False

Contract:
Comparison is case-sensitive. Both strings may be empty.

name: Challenge 05
title: CHALLENGE 5
statement:
CHALLENGE 5

A configuration language uses three kinds of brackets to open and close
blocks: ( ), [ ], and { }. A configuration string is well-formed only
if every block that opens is closed by the matching bracket, and blocks
are closed in the reverse order they were opened. Given such a string
(containing only bracket characters), return True if it is well-formed.

Examples:
    well_formed("{[()]}")  -> True
    well_formed("{[(])}")  -> False
    well_formed("(()")     -> False

Contract:
The empty configuration is well-formed. Return a bool.

CHALLENGE 6

title: CHALLENGE 7

CHALLENGE 7

A gift-card checkout lets a customer combine exactly two products whose
prices add up to the full balance on their card, leaving nothing unspent.
Given the list of product prices (in order on the page) and the card
balance, return the indices of the two products that sum to the balance.

Return the two indices as a list [i, j] with i < j. There is at most one
valid pair; if no pair works, return an empty list.

Examples:
    pair_for_total([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) -> [0, 1]
    pair_for_total([3, 2, 4], 6)      -> [1, 2]

Contract:
Prices and balance are integers. Each index can be used at most once.
Indices start at 0; empty lists are allowed.

CHALLENGE 8

        -> [["abc", "bca"], ["xyz"]]

Contract:
Codes are strings; comparison is case-sensitive. Empty codes and an
empty list are allowed. Keep repeated codes in the output.
